What Existing Research Studies: Taxonomies and design principles for what should be traced/logged/monitored in LLM and agent systems (artifacts, developer needs).
Typical Methods: Systematic mapping studies; qualitative focus groups/surveys.
Infrastructure vs. Semantic Signals Comp: Partially discussed conceptually, not empirically compared
What Remains Missing: No empirical test of whether any cataloged signal actually detects a semantic regression while infrastructure telemetry stays healthy.
Strength of Evidence: Moderate — consistent taxonomic findings across 2 independent sources, but neither is empirical.

What Existing Research Studies: Frameworks for recovering/inspecting agent reasoning traces and taxonomizing agent-internal failure modes (memory, planning, reflection, action).
Typical Methods: Prompt attribution; modular error taxonomy; LLM-as-judge trace debugging; annotated failure-trajectory datasets.
Models and Datasets Commonly Used: MMLU, SWE-bench Lite (Watson); ALFWorld, GAIA, WebShop (AgentDebug); mixed single/multi-agent traces (TRAIL).
What Remains Missing: These frameworks debug agent-internal reasoning, not serving-layer deployment faults (chat template, tokenizer, adapter, quantization, routing); TRAIL shows LLM-judge trace debugging is currently unreliable (11% best-case accuracy), a caution for detector design.
Strength of Evidence: Moderate-to-strong — three independent, recent (2025) papers converge on agent-failure taxonomies, but none addresses serving-layer faults.

What Existing Research Studies: Case studies and tools showing LLM API/model updates and prompt changes cause silent performance regressions; interactive tools to help developers find such regressions faster.
Typical Methods: Case-study analysis; interactive error-discovery tooling with human-in-the-loop comparison; metamorphic testing.
Models and Datasets Commonly Used: Toxicity-detection case study (CAIN 2024); mixed migration scenarios (RETAIN, EMNLP 2024 Demo); 3 unspecified LLMs, ~560K metamorphic tests (ICSME 2025).
What Remains Missing: Regression testing here is human-assisted and reactive (post-hoc discovery), not a continuous, automated, low-cost canary protocol run against a live serving deployment.
Strength of Evidence: Strong for motivating the problem (P004 is a direct, on-topic case study); weak for a ready-made detection solution.

What Existing Research Studies: Interactive/human-assisted tools for comparing model versions during migration; general (non-LLM-specific) statistical frameworks for online, temporal-dependence-aware deviation detection; multivocal and focus-group evidence that practitioners struggle to operationalize continuous quality monitoring for deployed ML systems in practice.
Typical Methods: Interactive tooling with human-in-the-loop error discovery; sequential online monitoring statistics; multivocal literature synthesis; qualitative focus-group study.
Models and Datasets Commonly Used: See RETAIN above; general ML-monitoring literature is not model-specific.
Online or Offline Evaluation?: Offline (RETAIN) / Online (P042's statistical framework, model-agnostic) / Conceptual (P039, P040)
False Alarms / Monitoring Cost Measured?: Partially (RETAIN reports time-to-discovery/effort proxies; P042 addresses false-alarm reduction statistically but not on LLM outputs)
What Remains Missing: No paper reviewed evaluates an always-on, low-cost, automated continuous-evaluation loop against production infrastructure constraints specifically for LLM semantic quality; P040's practitioner focus-group finding that 'production ML systems fail silently through wrong decisions' is the closest real-world corroboration of the SemaFailBench motivation found in this review, but it is general-ML and proposes no testable method.
Strength of Evidence: Moderate — the general-ML monitoring gap is now well-evidenced by three additional 2023-2025 sources (P039, P040, P042), but zero papers found test continuous evaluation specifically for LLM output semantics in production.

What Existing Research Studies: Chat templates measurably affect safety alignment, context-awareness, output diversity, and raw task accuracy; effects are large (up to 76 accuracy points) and can be exploited adversarially or arise incidentally.
Typical Methods: Controlled prompt/template perturbation; attention-allocation analysis; adversarial-attack construction; diversity/consistency evaluation (FormatSpread).
Models and Datasets Commonly Used: GPT-4 (Japanese case study); LLaMA-2-13B and other open-source LLMs (FormatSpread); 8 SOTA LLMs (ChatBug); open-source LLMs of varying size (context-awareness paper).
What Remains Missing: All reviewed papers study template sensitivity as a static/adversarial property; none tests the specific SemaFailBench scenario of a serving pipeline silently applying an incorrect or mismatched template to an already-deployed model while infrastructure metrics stay normal.
Strength of Evidence: Strong — six independent papers converge on large, reproducible chat-template effects; this is the best-evidenced fault category in the review.

What Existing Research Studies: Tokenizer vocabulary construction and segmentation choices materially affect quality, especially for non-English/non-Latin-script languages; adversarial datasets can specifically target tokenization weaknesses.
Typical Methods: Tokenization-mechanics analysis; adversarial dataset construction (ADT); efficiency-oriented vocabulary redesign.
Models and Datasets Commonly Used: GPT-4/GPT-4o (Problematic Tokens); GPT-4o, Llama-3, DeepSeek-R1 (ADT); unspecified tokenizers (conversation-optimized tokenizer study).
What Remains Missing: None of the reviewed tokenizer papers tests a deployment-time tokenizer/model version mismatch (e.g., wrong tokenizer file loaded at serving time) — all study tokenizer properties as trained/designed, not as an operational fault.
Strength of Evidence: Moderate — real, reproducible findings, but only 3 papers and none addresses the deployment-mismatch scenario directly; two of three have unverified author lists in this pass.

What Existing Research Studies: Systems research on scalable multi-adapter serving (S-LoRA) establishes the architecture in which adapter mismatches would occur; case-study evidence that silent model/API version changes cause regressions.
Typical Methods: Systems throughput benchmarking (S-LoRA); case-study regression analysis (CAIN 2024 paper).
Models and Datasets Commonly Used: General LoRA-adapted LLMs; commercial LLM APIs (toxicity case study).
Infrastructure vs. Semantic Signals Comp: Yes for S-LoRA (throughput only, not correctness) / No for the regression case study
What Remains Missing: No paper reviewed verifies that the *correct* adapter or model revision was actually applied and detects when it was not, despite serving infrastructure (S-LoRA-style) supporting many concurrent adapters; the general software-engineering mismatch taxonomy (P036) provides a structural precedent (misaligned assumptions between roles/components) that generalizes to this exact scenario but was never applied to adapter/version correctness specifically.
Strength of Evidence: Weak-to-moderate — the serving architecture is well studied and a generalizable SE mismatch framework exists (P036), but adapter/version-correctness verification itself appears to remain an open, unaddressed gap in the papers found.

What Existing Research Studies: Quantization can degrade safety alignment, introduce bias, disproportionately harm non-English/non-Latin-script languages, and have at least two distinguishable failure modes; automatic metrics can severely underestimate human-perceived degradation.
Typical Methods: Human + automatic safety benchmarking (OpenMiniSafety); BBQ bias benchmarking across precision levels; automatic + LLM-judge + human triangulated evaluation (multilingual); comparative PTQ-component evaluation.
Models and Datasets Commonly Used: 4 LLMs x 66 quantized variants (OpenMiniSafety); 3 instruction-tuned models x 5 precision levels (bias paper, unverified in this pass); multiple multilingual LLMs (EMNLP Findings 2024 paper).
What Remains Missing: All quantization studies compare quantization methods or precision levels on static benchmarks; none tests whether a lightweight canary could catch a quantization-induced regression in a live serving deployment where GPU/latency/throughput metrics remain nominal — directly the SemaFailBench premise, and P024's automatic-vs-human metric gap is the strongest single piece of supporting evidence found.
Strength of Evidence: Strong overall for the existence and severity of the problem (P024 especially); two entries (P022, P023) could not be fully verified from primary source text in this pass and should be treated cautiously.

What Existing Research Studies: Decoding parameters (temperature, top-p) are known informally to affect output quality and stability, and reasoning-stability research shows repeated-sampling instability is under-measured by single-run accuracy; but even after a dedicated second-pass search across 8 targeted query variants (temperature/top-p drift, generation-config regressions, stop-sequence failures, max-token truncation, sampling drift), this review still did not surface a paper directly studying decoding-configuration drift as a *deployment/serving-layer* fault with controlled injection.
Typical Methods: Not established from papers directly verified in this pass (for the deployment-fault framing specifically); G-Pass@k (P046) offers a reusable multi-sample stability-scoring method that was designed for a different purpose (reasoning-capability evaluation).
Models and Datasets Commonly Used: Not established from papers directly verified in this pass; G-Pass@k evaluated on math-reasoning LLMs (LiveMathBench).
What Remains Missing: This remains the weakest-covered fault category across both search passes; decoding-sensitivity papers surfaced in search were almost entirely about *designing better* adaptive/dynamic decoding algorithms or *measuring intrinsic* reasoning stability, not deployment-configuration drift as an operational fault. This should be explicitly disclosed as an unresolved literature gap in the manuscript rather than implied to be well-covered.
Supporting Paper IDs: (none meeting inclusion bar as a direct deployment-fault study; P046 is a partially-relevant adjacent methodology source)
Strength of Evidence: Weak — confirmed as a persisting gap after a dedicated targeted second-pass search; flagged as a priority for a follow-up MLSys/USENIX-specific search before manuscript finalization.

What Existing Research Studies: Embedding-space drift detection is an effective, low-overhead signal for detecting anomalous inputs in an adjacent problem (prompt-injection defense), with reported >93% accuracy and <3% false-positive rate.
What Remains Missing: The only semantic-drift paper found with a quantified false-positive rate applies the method to adversarial prompt-injection detection, not benign deployment-induced regression detection; this is a direct methodology-transfer opportunity for SemaFailBench rather than a competing benchmark.
Strength of Evidence: Weak coverage of the on-topic case, but the one paper found is methodologically strong and directly reusable (rare in this review to find a reported false-positive rate at all).

What Existing Research Studies: No paper meeting this review's inclusion bar was found that defines and evaluates "semantic canary prompts" specifically for LLM serving-deployment health monitoring (as opposed to prompt-format sensitivity benchmarking).
Typical Methods: Not established from papers directly verified in this pass.
Models and Datasets Commonly Used: Not established from papers directly verified in this pass.
What Remains Missing: This appears to be the central open gap SemaFailBench addresses: adjacent literature (chat-template sensitivity, IFEval-style verifiable instructions, POSIX-style sensitivity indices, FormatSpread) supplies building blocks, but no reviewed paper assembles them into a canary-based production-monitoring protocol with false-alarm, delay, and cost analysis.
Supporting Paper IDs: P006, P010, P021, P026 (building blocks only, not a direct competitor)
Strength of Evidence: Weak (as expected) — supports rather than undermines the novelty claim, pending the fuller search described in the Search Log.

What Existing Research Studies: Non-English and especially non-Latin-script languages are disparately and often more severely affected by tokenizer design and quantization; findings on whether English-only calibration disproportionately harms multilingual performance are not unanimous across the papers reviewed.
Typical Methods: Human + automatic + LLM-judge triangulated evaluation; tokenization-mechanics analysis; comparative calibration-set studies.
Models and Datasets Commonly Used: GPT-4/4o (tokenizer bias); multiple multilingual LLMs (EMNLP Findings 2024 quantization paper); unspecified (K-quantization calibration paper, unverified in this pass).
What Remains Missing: No paper reviewed evaluates multilingual degradation as a continuously monitored production signal; all are static benchmark comparisons, and at least one direct disagreement exists in the literature (P012/P024 vs. P025) that SemaFailBench's controlled design could help adjudicate; two large new multilingual capability benchmarks (BenchMAX, MMLU-ProX) confirm cross-linguistic performance gaps persist for advanced capabilities but, like the earlier entries, do not connect these gaps to deployment-time faults.
Strength of Evidence: Moderate-to-strong — real and important effects are now documented across six independent sources, but with at least one unresolved internal disagreement (P012/P024 vs. P025) and no paper anywhere in this review testing whether multilingual gaps widen specifically under a deployment fault.

What Existing Research Studies: Constrained-decoding frameworks can largely guarantee JSON-schema compliance, but a documented reliability gap exists between schema compliance and correct field-level values; deterministic, rule-checkable instruction formats (IFEval-style) exist and are reusable as automated canaries; training-time schema-reinforcement-learning methods can narrow (but do not eliminate discussion of) the compliance-vs-accuracy gap.
Typical Methods: Constrained-decoding benchmark evaluation (JSONSchemaBench); rule-based verifiable-instruction checking (IFEval); schema-reinforcement-learning training method (P043).
Models and Datasets Commonly Used: Six constrained-decoding frameworks across 10K real-world JSON schemas (JSONSchemaBench); two unspecified LLMs on ~500 verifiable-instruction prompts (IFEval); schema-RL-trained models (P043, exact list not itemized in this pass).
What Remains Missing: None of the three papers connects structured-output or instruction-following failures to underlying deployment faults (chat template, adapter, quantization) or evaluates them as a continuously-run production canary — all three supply directly reusable, low-cost, automatically-scorable canary formats and training precedents for SemaFailBench, but none tests whether structured-output reliability degrades after a deployment-time configuration change.
Strength of Evidence: Moderate-to-strong as a source of reusable canary formats and training precedent, though none of the three papers is itself a deployment-monitoring study.

What Existing Research Studies: Quantization (both PTQ and QAT) can degrade safety alignment and induce bias in a dose-response relationship with precision reduction; no single quantization method reliably preserves safety across settings.
Typical Methods: Human + automatic safety benchmarking (OpenMiniSafety); bias-benchmark scoring across precision levels.
Models and Datasets Commonly Used: 4 LLMs x 66 quantized variants; 3 instruction-tuned models x 5 precision levels (unverified in this pass).
What Remains Missing: Safety-alignment regression from quantization is documented as a static-benchmark phenomenon; no paper reviewed tests whether a safety-focused canary suite could detect such regression in a live deployment under normal infrastructure telemetry.
Strength of Evidence: Moderate — P016 is well-verified and directly relevant; P023's primary-source text could not be confirmed in this pass and should be treated cautiously until re-verified.

What Existing Research Studies: Established practices for holistic, multi-metric, multi-scenario LLM evaluation (HELM) and for deterministic, verifiable-instruction evaluation (IFEval) provide methodological precedent, but both evaluate static model releases offline rather than live serving deployments.
Typical Methods: Multi-metric standardized benchmarking; rule-based verifiable-instruction scoring; adversarial-prompt robustness benchmarking; LLM-as-judge survey.
Models and Datasets Commonly Used: 30 prominent LMs across 42 scenarios (HELM); 2 LLMs on ~500 IFEval prompts; multiple LLMs across 8 tasks/13 datasets (PromptRobust).
What Remains Missing: None of the general-purpose benchmark-design papers reviewed addresses continuous, low-cost, production-deployment monitoring under a constraint that infrastructure telemetry remains healthy — this is the specific methodological gap SemaFailBench's evaluation protocol is designed to fill.
Strength of Evidence: Strong as methodological precedent (well-established, widely cited practices), but none is a direct competitor to SemaFailBench's specific benchmark design.

What Existing Research Studies: Modern LLM serving stacks (vLLM/PagedAttention, SGLang) achieve large throughput/memory gains through architectural innovations (paged KV-cache, RadixAttention, structured-decoding runtimes), and a recent survey maps the broader systems-optimization landscape since 2023 — but this entire literature is organized around throughput, latency, and memory efficiency, not output-correctness verification.
Typical Methods: Systems benchmarking (throughput/latency under controlled workloads); survey synthesis of systems-optimization techniques.
Models and Datasets Commonly Used: Comparisons against FasterTransformer and Orca (vLLM); agentic/RAG/structured-output/multi-turn workloads (SGLang); broad survey scope, not model-specific (P049).
What Remains Missing: By omission, this is itself evidence for SemaFailBench's research gap: a comprehensive, recent (2024) survey of LLM serving-systems advances (P049) contains no discussion of semantic-quality or correctness monitoring, and neither foundational serving-stack paper (vLLM, SGLang) includes any correctness-verification layer — these systems could report perfectly healthy latency/throughput/GPU-utilization metrics while silently serving semantically degraded outputs due to a misconfiguration layered on top (wrong adapter, wrong chat template, wrong quantization).
Strength of Evidence: Strong for establishing that the dominant serving-systems research agenda is throughput/memory-focused and does not address output correctness — this is corroborating (not undermining) evidence for SemaFailBench's premise, drawn from the field's own most-cited systems papers.

What Existing Research Studies: A recent (2026) structured literature review synthesizing 48 sources proposes a 33-failure-mode taxonomy across the full RAG pipeline (ingestion through agentic orchestration) with explicit evidence grading, finding retrieval and generation failures comparatively well-studied while representation, evaluation, and agentic-orchestration failures remain an 'evidence desert.'
Typical Methods: Structured literature review with three-level evidence grading (Strong/Moderate/Limited) per failure mode.
Models and Datasets Commonly Used: Not model-specific (structured literature review of 48 sources).
What Remains Missing: This taxonomy is scoped specifically to RAG pipelines, not general LLM-serving deployment faults (chat template, tokenizer, adapter, quantization, decoding, routing); it does not itself propose or test a canary-based detection protocol, nor require an infrastructure-health constraint. Its methodology (taxonomy + evidence grading + explicit gap identification) is the closest precedent found in this entire review for SemaFailBench's own intended structure.
Strength of Evidence: Moderate — a single but methodologically rigorous and very recent (2026, workshop-peer-reviewed) source; RAG/retrieval-specific coverage should be treated as adjacent-but-distinct from SemaFailBench's general-serving-fault scope rather than as a direct competitor.

What Existing Research Studies: Only one paper meeting this review's inclusion bar directly concerns LLM routing mechanisms, and it studies *adversarial* exploitation of Mixture-of-Experts routing (steering queries to weakly aligned experts to elicit harmful content) via input-only, black-box-compatible attacks — not accidental/benign routing or version-mismatch faults (e.g., a load balancer serving the wrong model version or checkpoint).
Typical Methods: Adversarial-attack construction and evaluation against MoE routing.
Models and Datasets Commonly Used: MoE-architecture LLMs (exact list not itemized in this pass).
Controlled Faults Injected?: No (studies deliberate attack, not accidental fault)
What Remains Missing: This is one of the weakest-covered fault categories in the review even after a dedicated targeted search: no paper was found studying accidental/benign model-routing or version/checkpoint mismatches (the SemaFailBench 'model routing mistakes' fault category) as a deployment-monitoring problem; the one routing paper found does demonstrate that routing state is externally observable/inferable from outside a black-box serving system, which is methodologically useful for designing routing-fault canaries.
Strength of Evidence: Weak — confirmed as a persisting, disclosed gap; SemaFailBench's routing-fault canaries would need to be designed largely without a directly on-topic empirical precedent.

What Existing Research Studies: A recent (Findings of ACL 2025) paper shows single-sample accuracy substantially overstates real-world reliable reasoning ability; a multi-sample stability metric (G-Pass@k) reveals models are frequently unstable across repeated attempts at the same problem, even when peak performance is high.
Typical Methods: Multi-sample continuous evaluation metric (G-Pass@k) combined with a dynamic, leakage-resistant benchmark (LiveMathBench).
Models and Datasets Commonly Used: Multiple LLMs on dynamic, contemporary math problems.
What Remains Missing: Demonstrates output instability as an intrinsic model property measurable via repeated sampling on a fixed, unchanged deployment; does not test whether stability metrics shift detectably when a deployment fault (decoding-config change, quantization, adapter swap) is introduced, nor evaluate this in an online monitoring setting — a repeated-sampling, stability-aware scoring approach is nonetheless a strong candidate building block for SemaFailBench's canary scoring, to distinguish genuine deployment-induced regression from ordinary sampling variance.
Strength of Evidence: Moderate — a single, ACL-peer-reviewed, methodologically strong source; directly reusable as a scoring-methodology building block even though it does not test the deployment-fault scenario itself.
